title: Red Envelope Emoji 🧧 Meaning: Lunar New Year Lucky Money
description: The red envelope emoji 🧧 is the hongbao or lai see, money given for luck at Lunar New Year, weddings and birthdays. Learn the customs and how people use it in chats.
summary: 🧧 is a red envelope, called hóngbāo in Mandarin and lai see in Cantonese, which holds a gift of money for luck. It is sent most around Lunar New Year, but also at weddings, birthdays and other happy occasions. Online it means blessings, lucky money or, jokingly, “pay me.”
meaning: In Chinese and many other East and Southeast Asian communities, red stands for luck and celebration, and money handed over in a red envelope carries good wishes along with the cash. At Lunar New Year, married adults and elders traditionally give envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, who greet them with New Year wishes in return. Vietnamese families have a parallel custom at Tết called lì xì.

The details matter to people who practice it. Fresh, crisp bills are preferred, amounts are often even numbers, and the number four is avoided because it sounds like the word for death in Chinese. Envelopes are given and received with both hands. Red envelopes are strictly for joyful events; for funerals, a white envelope is used instead.

Digital red envelopes moved the custom onto phones. Messaging and payment apps such as WeChat and Alipay let users send money in a red envelope design, and group chats hold games where a sum is split randomly among whoever taps first. That is where 🧧 lives most naturally online: in holiday greetings, in group chats racing to grab a share, and in posts celebrating the season.

Outside the holiday, the emoji is used playfully. A friend who just got paid might be told “🧧 please,” and someone whose bet came good may post it to show lucky money arriving. The tone stays festive rather than greedy, because the envelope itself is a gift. It is a wish for someone else’s good fortune as much as a symbol of cash.

contexts.label: On holidays
contexts.body: Around Lunar New Year, 🧧 fills greetings, family photos and brand campaigns, often beside 🐉, 🏮 and 🍊. It goes with phrases such as Gong Xi Fa Cai or Xin Nian Kuai Le. Families abroad use it to send wishes across time zones, sometimes along with a digital envelope through a payment app.

contexts.label: Around the world
contexts.body: The custom is strongest in mainland China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam, and in diaspora communities worldwide. Malaysian Muslims have a related green envelope tradition for Eid, called duit raya, though the emoji itself is red. In each place, the envelope means good fortune passed from one generation to the next.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: Between friends, 🧧 is used for weddings, birthdays and new jobs, standing in for a gift or a wish of prosperity. It also features in the jokey “where’s my 🧧” that younger relatives send to aunts and uncles. In group chats it can announce that someone has dropped a digital envelope to grab.

confusedWith.difference: ✉️ is a plain letter envelope for mail, email and messages. 🧧 is specifically a red gift envelope for money and blessings, tied to Lunar New Year and celebrations.
🎁 is a wrapped present for birthdays, holidays and surprises in general. 🧧 is also a gift, but it holds money and belongs to a specific cultural tradition of luck.
💸 is cash flying away, meaning spending, losing money or paying out. 🧧 is money arriving as a gift, with good fortune attached.

avoid: Do not use it for condolences or funerals, where red envelopes are inappropriate and a white envelope is the custom.
Avoid treating it as a generic Asian decoration in contexts unrelated to the celebration, which can come across as careless.
design: A rectangular red envelope with gold detailing. Many versions show a gold emblem, pattern or seal on the front, echoing the printed characters and motifs found on real envelopes. The overall look is consistent across platforms: red and gold, compact, and flap at the top.

faqs.q: What does 🧧 mean from a friend?
faqs.a: Usually a festive wish for luck and prosperity, especially around Lunar New Year. It can also mean they are sending money, or jokingly asking for some, such as when you mention a bonus. Either way, it is friendly and upbeat.

faqs.q: Who gives red envelopes and who gets them?
faqs.a: Traditionally, married adults and elders give them to children and unmarried younger relatives at Lunar New Year. Employers may give them to staff, and guests give them to couples at weddings. Customs vary by family and region.

faqs.q: How much money goes in a red envelope?
faqs.a: There is no single rule. Many people choose even amounts, favor numbers with lucky sounds such as eight, and avoid four. New, crisp bills are preferred. The amount often depends on how close the relationship is.

faqs.q: What is a digital red envelope?
faqs.a: It is a feature in messaging and payment apps, such as WeChat and Alipay, that sends money wrapped in a red envelope design. In group chats, the sum can be split randomly among the first people to open it, which turns the gift into a game.

faqs.q: When was the red envelope emoji added?
faqs.a: 🧧 joined the emoji set in 2018, as part of emoji version 11.0, along with the firecracker. Before then people improvised with ✉️ or 💰 when wishing a happy Lunar New Year.
